([Adobe Firefly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adobe_Firefly "Adobe Firefly")).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-100) Many generative AI models are also available as [open-source software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software"), including Stable Diffusion and the LLaMA[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-101) language model.

Smaller generative AI models with up to a few billion parameters can run on [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphones "Smartphones"), embedded devices, and [personal computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computers "Personal computers"). For example, LLaMA-7B (a version with 7 billion parameters) can run on a [Raspberry Pi 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry_Pi_4 "Raspberry Pi 4")[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-102) and one version of Stable Diffusion can run on an [iPhone 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_11 "IPhone 11").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-103)

Larger models with tens of billions of parameters can run on [laptop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") or [desktop computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desktop_computers "Desktop computers"). To achieve an acceptable speed, models of this size may require [accelerators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_accelerator "AI accelerator") such as the [GPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPU "GPU") chips produced by [NVIDIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NVIDIA "NVIDIA") and [AMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMD "AMD") or the Neural Engine included in [Apple silicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_silicon "Apple silicon") products. For example, the 65 billion parameter version of LLaMA can be configured to run on a desktop PC.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-104)

The advantages of running generative AI locally include protection of [privacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_privacy "Information privacy") and [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property"), and avoidance of [rate limiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_limiting "Rate limiting") and [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship "Censorship"). The [subreddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit") r/LocalLLaMA in particular focuses on using [consumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_electronics "Consumer electronics")-grade gaming [graphics cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_card "Graphics card")[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-105) through such techniques as [compression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model#Compression "Large language model"). That forum is one of only two sources [Andrej Karpathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrej_Karpathy "Andrej Karpathy") trusts for [language model benchmarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_model#Evaluation_and_benchmarks "Language model").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-106)[Yann LeCun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yann_LeCun "Yann LeCun") has advocated open-source models for their value to [vertical applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_market_software "Vertical market software")[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-107) and for improving [AI safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety "AI safety").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-108)

Language models with hundreds of billions of parameters, such as GPT-4 or [PaLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PaLM "PaLM"), typically run on [datacenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datacenter "Datacenter") computers equipped with arrays of [GPUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPUs "GPUs") (such as NVIDIA's [H100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopper_(microarchitecture) "Hopper (microarchitecture)")) or [AI accelerator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_accelerator "AI accelerator") chips (such as Google's [TPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_Processing_Unit "Tensor Processing Unit")). These very large models are typically accessed as [cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") services over the Internet.

In 2022, the [United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China "United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China") imposed restrictions on exports to China of [GPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPU "GPU") and AI accelerator chips used for generative AI.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-109) Chips such as the NVIDIA A800[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-110) and the [Biren Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biren_Technology "Biren Technology") BR104[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-111) were developed to meet the requirements of the sanctions.

There is free software on the market capable of recognizing text generated by generative artificial intelligence (such as [GPTZero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPTZero "GPTZero")), as well as images, audio or video coming from it.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-112) Potential mitigation strategies for [detecting generative AI content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_content_detection "Artificial intelligence content detection") include [digital watermarking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_watermarking "Digital watermarking"), [content authentication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_provenance "Data provenance"), [information retrieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval "Information retrieval"), and [machine learning classifier models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervised_learning "Supervised learning").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-113) Despite claims of accuracy, both free and paid AI text detectors have frequently produced false positives, mistakenly accusing students of submitting AI-generated work.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-115)

### Generative models and training techniques

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Generative models and training techniques")]

#### Generative adversarial networks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Generative adversarial networks")]

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/GANs_Technique.webp/250px-GANs_Technique.webp.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GANs_Technique.webp)

Workflow for the training of a generative adversarial network.

[Generative adversarial networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network "Generative adversarial network") (GANs) are an influential generative modeling technique. GANs consist of two neural networks—the generator and the discriminator—trained simultaneously in a competitive setting. The generator creates [synthetic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data "Synthetic data") by transforming random noise into samples that resemble the training dataset. The discriminator is trained to distinguish the authentic data from synthetic data produced by the generator.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-116) The two models engage in a [minimax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimax "Minimax") game: the generator aims to create increasingly realistic data to "fool" the discriminator, while the discriminator improves its ability to distinguish real from fake data. This continuous training setup enables the generator to produce high-quality and realistic outputs.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-117)

#### Variational autoencoders

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Variational autoencoders")]

[![Image 11: Two images of the same cartoon crocodile](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/GAN_vs_VAE_%28cropped%29.png/500px-GAN_vs_VAE_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GAN_vs_VAE_(cropped).png)

Comparison between images generated by a VAE (left) and a GAN (right). VAEs tend to produce smoother but blurrier images due to their probabilistic decoding.

[Variational autoencoders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variational_autoencoder "Variational autoencoder") (VAEs) are deep learning models that probabilistically encode data. They are typically used for tasks such as [noise reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noise_reduction "Noise reduction") from images, [data compression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_compression "Data compression"), identifying unusual patterns, and [facial recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_recognition_system "Facial recognition system"). Unlike [standard autoencoders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoencoder "Autoencoder"), which compress input data into a fixed latent representation, VAEs model the [latent space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latent_space "Latent space") as a probability distribution,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-118) allowing for smooth sampling and interpolation between data points. The encoder ("recognition model") maps input data to a latent space, producing means and variances that define a probability distribution. The decoder ("generative model") samples from this latent distribution and attempts to reconstruct the original input. VAEs optimize a loss function that includes both the reconstruction error and a [Kullback–Leibler divergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kullback%E2%80%93Leibler_divergence "Kullback–Leibler divergence") term, which ensures the latent space follows a known prior distribution. VAEs are particularly suitable for tasks that require structured but smooth latent spaces, although they may create blurrier images than GANs. They are used for applications like image generation, data interpolation and [anomaly detection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomaly_detection "Anomaly detection").

[![Image 12: The full architecture of a GPT model.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Full_GPT_architecture.png/330px-Full_GPT_architecture.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Full_GPT_architecture.png)

The full architecture of a GPT model.

##### Transformers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Transformers")]

Transformers became the foundation for many powerful generative models, most notably the [generative pre-trained transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_pre-trained_transformer "Generative pre-trained transformer") (GPT) series developed by OpenAI. They marked a major shift in natural language processing by replacing traditional [recurrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network "Recurrent neural network") and [convolutional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") models.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-119) This architecture allows models to process entire sequences simultaneously and capture long-range dependencies more efficiently. The [self-attention mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_(machine_learning) "Attention (machine learning)") enables the model to capture the significance of every word in a sequence when predicting the subsequent word, thus improving its contextual understanding. Unlike recurrent neural networks, transformers process all the tokens in parallel, which improves the training efficiency and scalability. Transformers are typically pre-trained on enormous corpora in a [self-supervised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-supervised_learning "Self-supervised learning") manner, prior to being [fine-tuned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-tuning_(deep_learning) "Fine-tuning (deep learning)").

Law and regulation
------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Law and regulation")]

Main article: [Regulation of artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_artificial_intelligence "Regulation of artificial intelligence")

In the United States, a group of companies including OpenAI, Alphabet, and Meta signed a voluntary agreement with the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration") in July 2023 to watermark AI-generated content.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-120) In October 2023, [Executive Order 14110](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_14110 "Executive Order 14110") applied the [Defense Production Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Production_Act "Defense Production Act") to require all US companies to report information to the federal government when training certain high-impact AI models.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-122)

In the European Union, the proposed [Artificial Intelligence Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence_Act "Artificial Intelligence Act") includes requirements to disclose copyrighted material used to train generative AI systems, and to label any AI-generated output as such.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-124)

In China, the [Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interim_Measures_for_the_Management_of_Generative_AI_Services "Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services") introduced by the [Cyberspace Administration of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberspace_Administration_of_China "Cyberspace Administration of China") regulates any public-facing generative AI. It includes requirements to watermark generated images or videos, regulations on training data and label quality, restrictions on personal data collection, and a guideline that generative AI services must "adhere to socialist core values".[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-125)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-126)

### Copyright

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Copyright")]

Main article: [Artificial intelligence and copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_and_copyright "Artificial intelligence and copyright")

#### Training with copyrighted content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Training with copyrighted content")]

Generative AI systems such as [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT") and [Midjourney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midjourney "Midjourney") are trained on large, publicly available datasets that include copyrighted works. AI developers have argued that such training is protected under [fair use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_use "Fair use"), while copyright holders have argued that it infringes their rights.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-crscopyright-127)

Proponents of fair use training have argued that it is a [transformative use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformative_use "Transformative use") and does not involve making copies of copyrighted works available to the public.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-crscopyright-127) Critics have argued that image generators such as [Midjourney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midjourney "Midjourney") can create nearly-identical copies of some copyrighted images,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-128) and that generative AI programs compete with the content they are trained on.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-129)

As of 2024, several lawsuits related to the use of copyrighted material in training are ongoing. [Getty Images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getty_Images "Getty Images") has sued [Stability AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stability_AI "Stability AI") over the use of its images to train [Stable Diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-130) Both the [Authors Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authors_Guild "Authors Guild") and [The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times") have sued [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") and [OpenAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI") over the use of their works to train [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-131)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-132)

#### Copyright of AI-generated content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Copyright of AI-generated content")]

A separate question is whether AI-generated works can qualify for copyright protection. The [United States Copyright Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Copyright_Office "United States Copyright Office") has ruled that works created by artificial intelligence without any human input cannot be copyrighted, because they lack human authorship.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-133) Some legal professionals have suggested that _[Naruto v. Slater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey\_selfie\_copyright\_dispute "Monkey selfie copyright dispute")_ (2018), in which the [U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._9th_Circuit_Court_of_Appeals "U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals") held that [non-humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-human "Non-human") cannot be copyright holders of [artistic works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal-made_art "Animal-made art"), could be a potential precedent in copyright litigation over works created by generative AI.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-134) However, the office has also begun taking public input to determine if these rules need to be refined for generative AI.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-135)

In January 2025, the [United States Copyright Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Copyright_Office "United States Copyright Office") (USCO) released extensive guidance regarding the use of AI tools in the creative process, and established that "...generative AI systems also offer tools that similarly allow users to exert control. [These] can enable the user to control the selection and placement of individual creative elements. Whether such modifications rise to the minimum standard of originality required under [Feist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feist_Publications,_Inc.,_v._Rural_Telephone_Service_Co. "Feist Publications, Inc., v. Rural Telephone Service Co.") will depend on a case-by-case determination. In those cases where they do, the output should be copyrightable"[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-136) Subsequently, the USCO registered the first visual artwork to be composed of entirely AI-generated materials, titled "A Single Piece of American Cheese".[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-137)

Concerns
--------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Concerns")]

See also: [Ethics of artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics_of_artificial_intelligence "Ethics of artificial intelligence")

The development of generative AI has raised concerns from [governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government "Government"), businesses, and individuals, resulting in protests, legal actions, calls to [pause AI experiments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pause_Giant_AI_Experiments:_An_Open_Letter "Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter"), and actions by multiple governments. In a July 2023 briefing of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council"), [Secretary-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Secretary-General of the United Nations")[António Guterres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Guterres "António Guterres") stated "Generative AI has enormous potential for good and evil at scale", that AI may "turbocharge global development" and contribute between $10 and $15 trillion to the global economy by 2030, but that its malicious use "could cause horrific levels of death and destruction, widespread trauma, and deep psychological damage on an unimaginable scale".[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-138) In addition, generative AI has a significant [carbon footprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint").[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:82-139)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:14-140)

### Academic honesty

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Academic honesty")]

Generative AI can be used to generate and modify academic prose, to paraphrasing sources, and translate languages. The use of generative AI in a classroom setting can be a form of [academic plagiarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_dishonesty#Plagiarism "Academic dishonesty"). Some schools have banned ChatGPT and similar tools.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-Barrett-141)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-Chan2023-142)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS "Wikipedia:NOTRS")_]

A commonly proposed use for teachers is grading and giving feedback. Companies like Pearson and ETS use AI to score grammar, mechanics, usage, and style, but not for main ideas or overall structure.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-Barrett-141) The National Council of Teachers of English says machine scoring makes students feel their writing isn't worth reading.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-143) AI scoring has also given unfair results for students from different ethnic backgrounds.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-144)

### Job losses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Job losses")]

Main articles: [Workplace impact of artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workplace_impact_of_artificial_intelligence "Workplace impact of artificial intelligence") and [Technological unemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technological_unemployment "Technological unemployment")

[![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/AI_Protest_Sign_2023_WGA_Strike.jpg/250px-AI_Protest_Sign_2023_WGA_Strike.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AI_Protest_Sign_2023_WGA_Strike.jpg)

A picketer at the [2023 Writers Guild of America strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Writers_Guild_of_America_strike "2023 Writers Guild of America strike"). While not a top priority, one of the WGA's 2023 requests was "regulations around the use of (generative) AI".[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-145)

From the early days of the development of AI, there have been arguments put forward by [ELIZA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELIZA "ELIZA") creator [Joseph Weizenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum "Joseph Weizenbaum") and others about whether tasks that can be done by computers actually should be done by them, given the difference between computers and humans, and between quantitative calculations and qualitative, value-based judgements.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-146) In April 2023, it was reported that image generation AI has resulted in 70% of the jobs for video game illustrators in China being lost.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-147)[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-148) In July 2023, developments in generative AI contributed to the [2023 Hollywood labor disputes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Hollywood_labor_disputes "2023 Hollywood labor disputes"). [Fran Drescher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Drescher "Fran Drescher"), president of the [Screen Actors Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild "Screen Actors Guild"), declared that "artificial intelligence poses an existential threat to creative professions" during the [2023 SAG-AFTRA strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SAG-AFTRA_strike "2023 SAG-AFTRA strike").[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-149) Voice generation AI has been seen as a potential challenge to the [voice acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_acting "Voice acting") sector.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-150)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-151)

The intersection of AI and employment concerns among underrepresented groups globally remains a critical facet. While AI promises efficiency enhancements and skill acquisition, concerns about job displacement and biased recruiting processes persist among these groups, as outlined in surveys by [Fast Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Company "Fast Company"). To leverage AI for a more equitable society, proactive steps encompass mitigating biases, advocating transparency, respecting privacy and consent, and embracing diverse teams and ethical considerations. Strategies involve redirecting policy emphasis on regulation, inclusive design, and education's potential for personalized teaching to maximize benefits while minimizing harms.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-152)

### Racial and gender bias

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Racial and gender bias")]

Generative AI models can reflect and amplify any [cultural bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_bias "Cultural bias") present in the underlying data. For example, a language model might assume that doctors and judges are male, and that secretaries or nurses are female, if those biases are common in the training data.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-153) Similarly, an image model prompted with the text "a photo of a CEO" might disproportionately generate images of white male CEOs,[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-154) if trained on a racially biased data set. A number of methods for mitigating bias have been attempted, such as altering input prompts[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-155) and reweighting training data.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-DALL-E2-mitigations-156)

### Deepfakes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Deepfakes")]

Main article: [Deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake "Deepfake")

Deepfakes (a [portmanteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of "deep learning" and "fake"[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-FoxNews2018-157)) are AI-generated media that take a person in an existing image or video and replace them with someone else's likeness using [artificial neural networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_neural_network "Artificial neural network").[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:3-158) Deepfakes have garnered widespread attention and concerns for their uses in [deepfake celebrity pornographic videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake_pornography "Deepfake pornography"), [revenge porn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge_porn "Revenge porn"), [fake news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_news "Fake news"), [hoaxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax "Hoax"), health [disinformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinformation "Disinformation"), [financial fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accounting_scandals "Accounting scandals"), and covert [foreign election interference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_election_interference "Foreign election interference").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-HighSnobiety2018-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-160)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-164)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-165) This has elicited responses from both industry and government to detect and limit their use.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:21-166)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:5-167)

In July 2023, the fact-checking company [Logically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logically_(company) "Logically (company)") found that the popular generative AI models [Midjourney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midjourney "Midjourney"), [DALL-E 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DALL-E_2 "DALL-E 2") and [Stable Diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion") would produce plausible disinformation images when prompted to do so, such as images of [electoral fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud") in the United States and Muslim women supporting India's [Hindu nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_nationalist "Hindu nationalist")[Bharatiya Janata Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Janata_Party "Bharatiya Janata Party").[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-168)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-169)

In April 2024, a paper proposed to use [blockchain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain") ([distributed ledger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_ledger "Distributed ledger") technology) to promote "transparency, verifiability, and decentralization in AI development and usage".[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-170)

#### Audio deepfakes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Audio deepfakes")]

Main article: [Audio deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_deepfake "Audio deepfake")

Instances of users abusing software to generate controversial statements in the vocal style of celebrities, public officials, and other famous individuals have raised ethical concerns over voice generation AI.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-172)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:52-173)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-175)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:62-176) In response, companies such as ElevenLabs have stated that they would work on mitigating potential abuse through safeguards and [identity verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_document "Identity document").[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-engadget.com-177)

Concerns and fandoms have spawned from [AI-generated music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI-generated_music "AI-generated music"). The same software used to clone voices has been used on famous musicians' voices to create songs that mimic their voices, gaining both tremendous popularity and criticism.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-178)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-179)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-180) Similar techniques have also been used to create improved quality or full-length versions of songs that have been leaked or have yet to be released.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-181)

Generative AI has also been used to create new digital artist personalities, with some of these receiving enough attention to receive record deals at major labels.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-182) The developers of these virtual artists have also faced their fair share of criticism for their personified programs, including backlash for "dehumanizing" an artform, and also creating artists which create unrealistic or immoral appeals to their audiences.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-183)

### Illegal imagery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Illegal imagery")]

Main article: [Child pornography §Artificially generated or simulated imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_pornography#Artificially_generated_or_simulated_imagery "Child pornography")

Many websites that allow [explicit AI generated images or videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_pornography "AI pornography") have been created,[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-184) and this has been used to create illegal content, such as [rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_pornography "Rape pornography"), [child sexual abuse material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_sexual_abuse_material "Child sexual abuse material"),[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-185)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-186)[necrophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrophilia "Necrophilia"), and [zoophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoophilia "Zoophilia").

### Cybercrime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Cybercrime")]

Generative AI's ability to create realistic fake content has been exploited in numerous types of cybercrime, including [phishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phishing "Phishing") scams.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-187)[Deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake "Deepfake") video and audio have been used to create disinformation and fraud. In 2020, former Google [click fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Click_fraud "Click fraud") czar [Shuman Ghosemajumder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuman_Ghosemajumder "Shuman Ghosemajumder") argued that once deepfake videos become perfectly realistic, they would stop appearing remarkable to viewers, potentially leading to uncritical acceptance of false information.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-188) Additionally, [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") and other forms of text-generation AI have been used to create fake reviews of [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") websites to boost ratings.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-189) Cybercriminals have created large language models focused on fraud, including WormGPT and FraudGPT.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-190)

A 2023 study showed that generative AI can be vulnerable to jailbreaks, [reverse psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_psychology "Reverse psychology") and [prompt injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prompt_injection "Prompt injection") attacks, enabling attackers to obtain help with harmful requests, such as for crafting [social engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_engineering_(security) "Social engineering (security)") and [phishing attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phishing "Phishing").[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-191) Additionally, other researchers have demonstrated that open-source models can be [fine-tuned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-tuning_(deep_learning) "Fine-tuning (deep learning)") to remove their safety restrictions at low cost.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-192)

### Information laundering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Information laundering")]

Generative AI has been noted for its use by [state-sponsored propaganda campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-sponsored_Internet_propaganda "State-sponsored Internet propaganda") in [information laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_laundering "Information laundering"). According to a 2025 report by [Graphika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphika "Graphika"), generative AI is used to launder articles from Chinese [state media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_media "State media") such as [China Global Television Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Global_Television_Network "China Global Television Network") through various social media sites in an attempt to disguise the articles' origin.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:53-193)

### Reliance on industry giants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Reliance on industry giants")]

Training [frontier AI models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier_model "Frontier model") requires an enormous amount of computing power. Usually only [Big Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech "Big Tech") companies have the financial resources to make such investments. Smaller start-ups such as [Cohere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohere "Cohere") and [OpenAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI") end up buying access to [data centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_centers "Data centers") from [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google") and [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") respectively.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-194)

### Energy and environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Energy and environment")]

Main article: [Environmental impacts of artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impacts_of_artificial_intelligence "Environmental impacts of artificial intelligence")

AI has a significant carbon footprint due to growing energy consumption from both training and usage.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:82-139)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:14-140) Scientists and journalists have expressed concerns about the environmental impact that the development and deployment of generative models are having: high CO 2 emissions,[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:1-195)[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:2-196)[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197) large amounts of freshwater used for data centers,[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:9-199) and high amounts of electricity usage.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:2-196)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:11-201) There is also concern that these impacts may increase as these models are incorporated into widely used search engines such as Google Search and Bing,[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200) as [chatbots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatbot "Chatbot") and other applications become more popular,[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:9-199)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200) and as models need to be retrained.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200)

The carbon footprint of generative AI globally is estimated to be growing steadily, with potential annual emissions ranging from 18.21 to 245.94 million tons of CO 2 by 2035,[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-202) with the highest estimates for 2035 nearing the impact of the United States [beef industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beef_industry "Beef industry") on emissions (currently estimated to emit 257.5 million tons annually as of 2024).[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-203)

Proposed mitigation strategies include factoring potential environmental costs prior to model development or data collection,[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:1-195) increasing efficiency of data centers to reduce electricity/energy usage,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:11-201) building more efficient [machine learning models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"),[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:2-196)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:9-199) minimizing the number of times that models need to be retrained,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197) developing a government-directed framework for auditing the environmental impact of these models,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198) regulating for transparency of these models,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197) regulating their energy and water usage,[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198) encouraging researchers to publish data on their models' carbon footprint,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200) and increasing the number of subject matter experts who understand both machine learning and climate science.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)

### Content quality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Content quality")]

See also: [AI slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop "AI slop") and [Dead Internet theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Internet_theory "Dead Internet theory")

_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ defines [slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop "AI slop") as analogous to [spam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spamming "Spamming"): "shoddy or unwanted A.I. content in social media, art, books, and ... in search results."[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-204) Journalists have expressed concerns about the scale of low-quality generated content with respect to social media content moderation,[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:12-205) the monetary incentives from social media companies to spread such content,[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:12-205)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:13-206) false political messaging,[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:13-206) spamming of scientific research paper submissions,[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-207) increased time and effort to find higher quality or desired content on the Internet,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-208) the indexing of generated content by search engines,[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-209) and on journalism itself.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-210)

A paper published by researchers at Amazon Web Services AI Labs found that over 57% of sentences from a sample of over 6 billion sentences from [Common Crawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Crawl "Common Crawl"), a snapshot of web pages, were [machine translated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_translation "Machine translation"). Many of these automated translations were seen as lower quality, especially for sentences that were translated into at least three languages. Many lower-resource languages (ex. [Wolof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolof_language "Wolof language"), [Xhosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_language "Xhosa language")) were translated across more languages than higher-resource languages (ex. English, French).[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-211)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-212)

In September 2024, [Robyn Speer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Mind_Common_Sense "Open Mind Common Sense"), the author of wordfreq, an open source database that calculated word frequencies based on text from the Internet, announced that she had stopped updating the data for several reasons: high costs for obtaining data from [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit") and [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), excessive focus on generative AI compared to other methods in the [natural language processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing") community, and that "generative AI has polluted the data".[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-213)

The adoption of generative AI tools led to an explosion of AI-generated content across multiple domains. A study from [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London") estimated that in 2023, more than 60,000 scholarly articles—over 1% of all publications—were likely written with LLM assistance.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-214) According to [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University")'s Institute for Human-Centered AI, approximately 17.5% of newly published computer science papers and 16.9% of peer review text now incorporate content generated by LLMs.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-215) Many academic disciplines have concerns about the factual reliability of academic content generated by AI.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-216)

Visual content follows a similar trend. Since the launch of [DALL-E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DALL-E "DALL-E") 2 in 2022, it is estimated that an average of 34 million images have been created daily. As of August 2023, more than 15 billion images had been generated using text-to-image algorithms, with 80% of these created by models based on [Stable Diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion").[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-217)

If AI-generated content is included in new data crawls from the Internet for additional training of AI models, defects in the resulting models may occur.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-218) Training an AI model exclusively on the output of another AI model produces a lower-quality model. Repeating this process, where each new model is trained on the previous model's output, leads to progressive degradation and eventually results in a "[model collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_collapse "Model collapse")" after multiple iterations.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-219) Tests have been conducted with pattern recognition of handwritten letters and with pictures of human faces.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-220) As a consequence, the value of data collected from genuine human interactions with systems may become increasingly valuable in the presence of LLM-generated content in data crawled from the Internet.

On the other side, [synthetic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data "Synthetic data") is often used as an alternative to data produced by real-world events. Such data can be deployed to validate mathematical models and to train machine learning models while preserving user privacy,[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-221) including for structured data.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-222) The approach is not limited to text generation; image generation has been employed to train computer vision models.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-223)

### Misuse in journalism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Misuse in journalism")]

See also: [Automated journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_journalism "Automated journalism") and [List of fake news websites §Generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fake_news_websites#Generative_AI "List of fake news websites")

Generative AI's potential to generate a large amount of content with little effort is also affecting journalism.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-224) In January 2023, _[Futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism\_(website) "Futurism (website)")_ broke the story that [CNET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNET "CNET") had been using an undisclosed internal AI tool to write at least 77 of its stories; after the news broke, CNET posted corrections to 41 of the stories.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-225) In April 2023, _Die Aktuelle_ published an AI-generated fake interview of [Michael Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schumacher "Michael Schumacher").[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-226) In May 2024, _Futurism_ noted that a content management system video by AdVon Commerce, which had used generative AI to produce articles for many of the aforementioned outlets, appeared to show that they "had produced tens of thousands of articles for more than 150 publishers."[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-227) In 2025, a report from the American Sunlight Project stated that [Pravda network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pravda_network "Pravda network") was publishing as many as 10,000 articles a day, and concluded that much of this content aimed to push Russian narratives into [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") through their training data.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-228)

In June 2024, [Reuters Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters_Institute "Reuters Institute") published its _Digital News Report for 2024_. In a survey of people in America and Europe, Reuters Institute reports that 52% and 47% respectively are uncomfortable with news produced by "mostly AI with some human oversight", and 23% and 15% respectively report being comfortable. 42% of Americans and 33% of Europeans reported that they were comfortable with news produced by "mainly human with some help from AI". The results of global surveys reported that people were more uncomfortable with news topics including politics (46%), crime (43%), and local news (37%) produced by AI than other news topics.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-229)

Detection and awareness
-----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Detection and awareness")]

See also: [Artificial intelligence content detection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_content_detection "Artificial intelligence content detection")

Online users have falsely assumed media of using generative artificial intelligence for content, such as video games _Little Droid_ and _[Catly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catly "Catly")_.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-230)

Due to various concerns about citizens' unknowingly consuming generative AI media content, proponents argue for labeling such content to provide context. The [Cyberspace Administration of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberspace_Administration_of_China "Cyberspace Administration of China") issued rules obligating service providers to labeling this content online.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-231)

The popularity of ChatGPT caused the emergence of tools that detect whether content was AI-generated, such as [GPTZero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPTZero "GPTZero"), but the risk of false accusations ([false positives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positives_and_false_negatives "False positives and false negatives")) has remained a concern.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-232)[Digital watermarking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_watermarking "Digital watermarking") allows to reach high detection accuracy by subtly altering the generated content in a way that can be detected by software, but without being noticeable by users. OpenAI developed in 2023 a digital watermarking tool that allowed to detect content generated by [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT") with an estimated accuracy of 99.9%, when given enough text. But OpenAI chose not to release it, worrying that users would switch to competitor products, and arguing that digital watermarking can be circumvented by bad actors, for example with superficial rephrasing.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-233)[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-234) Google's digital watermarking tool called SynthID was integrated in 2025 into products like Gemini, Imagen and Veo. Google also created the portal SynthID detector for users to check whether text, images or videos were produced with Google's generative AI products.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-235)

# What is generative AI?

22 March 2024

Link copied

## Authors

[Cole Stryker](https://www.ibm.com/think/author/cole-stryker) 

Staff Editor, AI Models

IBM Think

[Mark Scapicchio](https://www.ibm.com/think/author/Mark-Scapicchio) 

Editor, Topics & Insights

IBM Think

## What is generative AI?

Generative AI, sometimes called *gen AI,* is [artificial intelligence](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence) (AI) that can create original content such as text, images, video, audio or software code in response to a user’s prompt or request.

Generative AI relies on sophisticated [machine learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/machine-learning) models called *[deep learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/deep-learning)* *models*algorithms that simulate the learning and decision-making processes of the human brain. These models work by identifying and encoding the patterns and relationships in huge amounts of data, and then using that information to understand users' natural language requests or questions and respond with relevant new content.

AI has been a hot technology topic for the past decade, but generative AI, and specifically the arrival of ChatGPT in 2022, has thrust AI into worldwide headlines and launched an unprecedented surge of AI innovation and adoption. Generative AI offers enormous productivity benefits for individuals and organizations, and while it also presents very real challenges and risks, businesses are forging ahead, exploring how the technology can improve their internal workflows and enrich their products and services. According to research by the management consulting firm McKinsey, one third of organizations are already using generative AI regularly in at least one business function.¹ Industry analyst Gartner projects more than 80% of organizations will have deployed generative AI applications or used generative AI application programming interfaces (APIs) by 2026.2

## How generative AI works

For the most part, generative AI operates in three phases:

* **Training**, to create a foundation model that can serve as the basis of multiple gen AI applications.
* **Tuning**, to tailor the foundation model to a specific gen AI application.
* **Generation**, **evaluation and retuning***,* to assess the gen AI application's output and continually improve its quality and accuracy.

Generative AI begins with a foundation model, a deep learning model that serves as the basis for multiple different types of generative AI applications. The most common foundation models today are [large language models (LLMs)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/large-language-models), created for text generation applications, but there are also foundation models for image generation, video generation, and sound and music generation as well as multimodal foundation models that can support several kinds content generation.

To create a foundation model, practitioners train a deep learning algorithm on huge volumes of raw, unstructured, unlabeled data e.g., terabytes of data culled from the internet or some other huge data source. During training, the algorithm performs and evaluates millions of ‘fill in the blank’ exercises, trying to predict the next element in a sequence e.g., the next word in a sentence, the next element in an image, the next command in a line of code and continually adjusting itself to minimize the difference between its predictions and the actual data (or ‘correct’ result).

The result of this training is a [neural network](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/neural-networks) of *parameters,*encoded representations of the entities, patterns and relationships in the data, that can generate content autonomously in response to inputs, or prompts.

This training process is compute-intensive, time-consuming and expensive: it requires thousands of clustered graphics processing units (GPUs) and weeks of processing, all of which costs millions of dollars. Open-source foundation model projects, such as Meta's Llama-2, enable gen AI developers to avoid this step and its costs.

### Tuning

Metaphorically speaking, a foundation model is a generalist: It knows a lot about a lot of types of content, but often can’t generate specific types of output with desired accuracy or fidelity. For that, the model must be tuned to a specific content generation task. This can be done in a variety of ways.

#### Fine tuning

[Fine tuning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/fine-tuning) involves feeding the model labeled data specific to the content generation application questions or prompts the application is likely to receive, and corresponding correct answers in the desired format. For example, if a development team is trying to create a customer service chatbot, it would create hundreds or thousands of documents containing labeled customers service questions and correct answers, and then feed those documents to the model.

Fine-tuning is labor-intensive. Developers often outsource the task to companies with large data-labeling workforces.

#### Reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF)

In [RLHF](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/rlhf), human users respond to generated content with evaluations the model can use to update the model for greater accuracy or relevance. Often, RLHF involves people ‘scoring’ different outputs in response to the same prompt. But it can be as simple as having people type or talk back to a chatbot or virtual assistant, correcting its output.

### Generation, evaluation, more tuning

Developers and users continually assess the outputs of their generative AI apps, and further tune the model even as often as once a week for greater accuracy or relevance. (In contrast, the foundation model itself is updated much less frequently, perhaps every year or 18 months.)

Another option for improving a gen AI app's performance is *retrieval augmented generation* (RAG). RAG is a framework for extending the foundation model to use relevant sources outside of the training data, to supplement and refine the parameters or representations in the original model.RAG can ensure that a generative AI app always has access to the most current information. As a bonus, the additional sources accessed via RAG are transparent to users in a way that the knowledge in the original foundation model is not.

## Generative AI model architectures and how they have evolved

Truly generative AI models deep learning models that can autonomously create content on demand have evolved over the last dozen years or so. The milestone model architectures during that period include

* **Variational autoencoders (VAEs)**, which drove breakthroughs in image recognition, natural language processing and anomaly detection.
* **Generative adversarial networks (GANs)** and **diffusion models**, which improved the accuracy of previous applications and enabled some of the first AI solutions for photo-realistic image generation.
* **Transformers**, the deep learning model architecture behind the foremost foundation models and generative AI solutions today.

### Variational autoencoders (VAEs)

An [autoencoder](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/autoencoder) is a deep learning model comprising two connected neural networks: One that encodes (or compresses) a huge amount of unstructured, unlabeled training data into parameters, and another that decodes those parameters to reconstruct the content. Technically, autoencoders can generate new content, but they’re more useful for compressing data for storage or transfer, and decompressing it for use, than they are for high-quality content generation.

Introduced in 2013, variational autoencoders (VAEs) can encode data like an autoencoder, but *decode multiple new variations of the content*. By training a VAE to generate variations toward a particular goal, it can ‘zero in’ on more accurate, higher-fidelity content over time. Early VAE applications included anomaly detection (e.g., medical image analysis) and natural language generation.

### Generative adversarial networks (GANs)

GANs, introduced in 2014, also comprise two neural networks: A generator, which generates new content, and a discriminator, which evaluates the accuracy and quality the generated data. These adversarial algorithms encourages the model to generate increasingly high-quality outpits.

GANs are commonly used for image and video generation, but can generate high-quality, realistic content across various domains. They've proven particularly successful at tasks as *style transfer* (altering the style of an image from, say, a photo to a pencil sketch) and *data augmentation* (creating new, synthetic data to increase the size and diversity of a training data set).

### Diffusion models

Also introduced in 2014, diffusion models work by first adding noise to the training data until it’s random and unrecognizable, and then training the algorithm to iteratively diffuse the noise to reveal a desired output.

Diffusion models take more time to train than VAEs or GANs, but ultimately offer finer-grained control over output, particularly for high-quality image generation tool. DALL-E, Open AI’s image-generation tool, is driven by a diffusion model.

### Transformers

First documented in a 2017 paper published by Ashish Vaswani and others, [transformers](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/transformer-model) evolve the encoder-decoder paradigm to enable a big step forward in the way foundation models are trained, and in the quality and range of content they can produce. These models are at the core of most of today’s headline-making generative AI tools, including ChatGPT and GPT-4, Copilot, BERT, Bard, and Midjourney to name a few.

Transformers use a concept called *attention,*determining and focusing on what’s most important about data within a sequence to;

* process entire sequences of data e.g., sentences instead of individual words simultaneously;
* capture the context of the data within the sequence;
* encode the training data into *embeddings* (also called *hyperparameters*) that represent the data and its context.

In addition to enabling faster training, transformers excel at natural language processing (NLP) and natural language understanding (NLU), and can generate longer sequences of data e.g., not just answers to questions, but poems, articles or papers with greater accuracy and higher quality than other deep generative AI models. Transformer models can also be trained or tuned to use tools e.g., a spreadsheet application, HTML, a drawing program to output content in a particular format.

## What generative AI can create

Generative AI can create many types of content across many different domains.

Text  

Generative models. especially those based on transformers, can generate coherent, contextually relevant text, everything from instructions and documentation to brochures, emails, web site copy, blogs, articles, reports, papers, and even creative writing. They can also perform repetitive or tedious writing tasks (e.g., such as drafting summaries of documents or meta descriptions of web pages), freeing writers’ time for more creative, higher-value work.

Images and video  

Image generation such as DALL-E, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion can create realistic images or original art, and can perform style transfer, image-to-image translation and other image editing or image enhancement tasks. Emerging gen AI video tools can create animations from text prompts, and can apply special effects to existing video more quickly and cost-effectively than other methods.

Sound, speech and music  

Generative models can synthesize natural-sounding speech and audio content for voice-enabled AI chatbots and digital assistants, audiobook narration and other applications. The same technology can generate original music that mimics the structure and sound of professional compositions.

Software code  

Gen AI can generate original code, autocomplete code snippets, translate between programming languages and summarize code functionality. It enables developers to quickly prototype, refactor, and debug applications while offering a natural language interface for coding tasks.

Design and art  

Generative AI models can generate unique works of art and design, or assist in graphic design. Applications include dynamic generation of environments, characters or avatars, and special effects for virtual simulations and video games.

Simulations and synthetic data  

Generative AI models can be trained to generate [synthetic data](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/synthetic-data), or synthetic structures based on real or synthetic data. For example, generative AI is applied in drug discovery to generate molecular structures with desired properties, aiding in the design of new pharmaceutical compounds.

## Benefits of generative AI

The obvious, overarching benefit of generative AI is **greater **e**fficiency**. Because it can generate content and answers on demand, gen AI has the potential to accelerate or automate labor-intensive tasks, cut costs, and free employees time for higher-value work.

But generative AI offers several other benefits for indivuduals and organizations.

### Enhanced creativity

Gen AI tools can inspire creativity through automated brainstorming, generating multiple novel versions of content. These variations can also serve as starting points or references that help writers, artists, designers and other creators plow through creative blocks.

### Improved (and faster) decision-making

Generative AI excels at analyzing large datasets, identifying patterns and extracting meaningful insights, then generating hypotheses and recommendations based on those insights to support executives, analysts, researchers and other professionals in making smarter, data-driven decisions.

### Dynamic personalization

In applications like recommendation systems and content creation, generative AI can analyze user preferences and history and generate personalized content in real time, leading to a more tailored and engaging user experience.

### Constant availability

Generative AI operates continuously without fatigue, providing around-the-clock availability for tasks like customer support [chatbots](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/chatbots) and automated responses.
